name: Toltec
summary: A Mesoamerican culture centred on Tula in central Mexico, at its height from 950 to 1150. The later Aztecs saw the Toltecs as their cultural ancestors.

location.value: Central Mexico, centred on Tula (Tollan) in Hidalgo.

terrain.value: Highland valleys north of the Valley of Mexico.

climate.value: Semi-arid highland climate, with a rainy summer.

resources.value: Maize, beans and maguey farming; obsidian from nearby sources.

disasters.value: Drought may have contributed to its decline.

population.value: Tula may have had about 30,000–60,000 people at its height.

urbanisation.value: Tula was a large planned city covering about 16 km².

migration.value: Northern peoples moved into central Mexico.

economicBase.value: Farming and crafts, especially obsidian tools.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade networks reaching as far as Chichén Itzá in Yucatán and the American Southwest (turquoise).

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute from surrounding towns; no coinage.

inequality.value: A warrior and priestly elite above farmers and craftspeople.

governmentType.value: A state ruled from Tula; its organisation is debated.

keyRulers.value: Aztec accounts name Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl, but scholars debate how historical these accounts are.

succession.value: Unknown; later Aztec legends name kings such as Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl.

institutions.value: Military orders of warriors associated with eagles and jaguars.

stability.value: Unknown in detail; Tula was a major city for about two centuries.

eliteConflict.value: Legends tell of a conflict between Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl and the god Tezcatlipoca’s followers.

armyAndTech.value: Warrior orders (eagles, jaguars) armed with spear-throwers (atlatl) and darts.

majorWars.value: Unknown; Tula was burned and looted around 1150.

territoryChange.value: Influence across central Mexico; how far its rule reached is debated.

alliancesRivals.value: Links with Chichén Itzá, which shares architectural styles with Tula.

scienceEducation.value: Unknown; the Aztecs later saw the Toltecs as masters of all arts and knowledge.

openness.value: Contact with the Maya and with peoples far to the north.

communicationTransport.value: Travel on foot along trade routes (no draft animals); porters carried goods.

religion.value: Worship of the feathered serpent Quetzalcoatl, Tezcatlipoca and other gods.

languageWriting.value: Nahuatl; the word Toltec came to mean “artisan”.

artsArchitecture.value: The Atlantean warrior columns on Pyramid B at Tula; chacmool statues.

sharedIdentity.value: Later seen by the Aztecs as the epitome of civilisation.

dailyLife.value: Stone and adobe houses in Tula; maize, beans, squash and maguey drinks.

neighbours.value: Maya, Huastec and other Mesoamerican peoples.

ideasReligions.value: Spread the cult of Quetzalcoatl; later rulers such as the Aztecs claimed Toltec descent.

riseSignals.value: Tula rose to prominence around 950, after the decline of Teotihuacan.

peakPeriod.value: About 950–1150, when Tula was the main city of central Mexico.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Toltec (checked 6 Nov 2026); Davies, The Toltecs (1977)

declineSignals.value: Drought, internal conflict and pressure from northern peoples.

outcome.value: Declined; later peoples, including the Aztecs, claimed Toltec heritage.

sources.value: Archaeology and Aztec traditions. Checked against Wikipedia (“Toltec”).

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. Scholars debate how far Aztec accounts are historical.

knownFor.label: Quetzalcoatl legend
knownFor.note: The feathered serpent and the priest-king.

knownFor.label: “Toltec” = artisan
knownFor.note: In Nahuatl the name came to mean skilled craftsman.
